# Raw Linux writes, errors and partial progress

This investigation connects a C function call to an actual Linux kernel write.
Predict the argument registers, observe the transferred bytes, compare the raw
error return with libc, then follow partial progress through an owned pipe.
The separate parser project remains the exercise for argument grammar and range.

## Target and complete role folders

Use Linux x86-64, the System V AMD64 function ABI, the Linux x86-64 syscall ABI,
GNU assembler Intel syntax, C17, CMake 3.20+, Clang or GCC, GDB and strace. Confirm
`uname -s` and `uname -m` before building. Windows uses an x86-64 WSL Linux
distribution; macOS uses an x86-64 Linux VM or lab. No administrator account is
needed for these programs.

Each role contains `routine.S`, `main.c`, `lab.h`, `tests.c`, `abi_checks.S`,
`CMakeLists.txt` and `trace.md`. Keep the selected role and this guide together.
Work in `starter`; save that attempt before opening the separate `solution`.
The browser edits, saves and exports the files. Build and run them in Linux.

The two roles differ only in `routine.S`. Complete the named `SYSCALL_WRITE`
task and the explanatory worksheet. Keep the C callers and checks unchanged.
The untouched routine returns a synthetic `-ENOSYS` value without making a
write syscall. The demo recognizes the missing behavior and exits 78 after
closing its own descriptors. Its contracts fail. A successful compilation is
therefore an initial observation, not completion.

## Two boundaries with different responsibilities

The exported C function is:

```c
long lab_write(long fd, const void *buffer, unsigned long count);
```

The caller supplies a readable buffer of at least `count` bytes and an owned
descriptor. For this three-argument function, RDI, RSI and RDX already hold the
arguments that Linux write needs. Select syscall number 1 in RAX and execute
the boundary instruction. RAX receives the result. RCX and R11 are clobbered
by that boundary; the function must still preserve RBX, RBP and R12–R15 and
return with the original stack state.

A nonnegative return counts actual bytes transferred. A negative return from
this wrapper is the raw kernel error value. This assembly function leaves C's
`errno` storage alone. In contrast, libc `write()` reports an error as -1 and
sets `errno` to its positive error code. Even libc's function named `syscall()`
performs library error conversion; it is distinct from the assembly instruction.

The same underlying failure can have different printed representations. GDB
shows the raw RAX value; strace normally formats a failed call as `-1 EBADF`.
That tracer notation does not establish that the assembly function changed
`errno`. Record the returned value and the separately captured C `errno` value.

## Predict the normal and invalid-descriptor cases

The default payload is `owned-kernel-bytes`, which has 18 bytes. The C driver
creates a pipe, sets an `errno` sentinel of 123, calls the assembly function,
then reads and compares the actual bytes. A completed first row is:

```text
raw bytes=18 errno=123 payload=owned-kernel-bytes
```

Next the driver passes descriptor -1 through both interfaces. The raw call
returns negative `EBADF` and preserves 123. The libc call returns -1 and sets
`errno` to `EBADF`. The output uses the target's numeric error values from
`errno.h`. Explain why the values are different without treating one as success.

The driver captures `errno` immediately after each call, before printing or
making another library call. Copy that observation order into the worksheet.
Changing the expected result or moving the sentinel after the call would erase
the comparison rather than implement the missing syscall.

## A successful call can transfer only part of the request

The driver next owns an empty nonblocking pipe and reads its actual capacity
with `F_GETPIPE_SZ`. This bounded fixture accepts capacities from 4096 through
65536 bytes and allocates a request twice that size. It initializes every byte
with a deterministic, nonconstant pattern.

For an observed capacity C, predict this sequence:

1. Request 2C bytes. The empty pipe accepts C, a positive short result.
2. Request one more byte while the pipe is full. The raw call returns `-EAGAIN`.
3. Drain C bytes and compare them with the original first segment.
4. Advance the source pointer by the actual first return, request the remaining
   C bytes, drain them and compare the complete 2C-byte observation.

The final row records requested, first, full-pipe error, remaining, total and
checked-byte counts. C comes from that run; it is not a hardcoded platform
promise. The `--changed` argument changes the small payload to
`changed-kernel-bytes` while retaining the partial-progress experiment.

Do not loop blindly after `EAGAIN`, add a negative error to the pointer, or
assume a positive result equals the requested count. The controlled driver
drains its own pipe to create progress. A general asynchronous writer would
also need a readiness and cancellation policy; this program makes no such
general-purpose claim. An unexpected return causes cleanup and a nonzero exit.

## Build, check and inspect

From the extracted project folder:

```sh
cmake -S starter -B build-first -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_ASM_COMPILER=clang
cmake --build build-first --parallel 1
ctest --test-dir build-first --output-on-failure
./build-first/app
```

Retain the untouched failures. Complete only the named assembly task, then use
a fresh `build-completed` directory with the same options. Require the contracts
and both `app` and `app --changed` to pass. Build `solution` independently in
`build-reference`. Repeat completed roles in Release and with both compiler
options set to `gcc`; use separate build folders.

The contracts use 65 different byte counts and binary payload bytes, check two
raw `EBADF` cases, preserve the `errno` sentinel and verify six callee-saved
registers through the supplied assembly checker. These checks remain active in
Release. The demo supplies the additional real short-write and full-pipe cases.

```sh
objdump -d -Mintel --disassemble=lab_write build-completed/app
strace -f -yy -s 131072 -e trace=write,read,pipe2,fcntl,close -o observed-write.strace ./build-completed/app
gdb ./build-completed/app
```

Use a fresh trace filename for each run. In GDB:

```text
set disassembly-flavor intel
break *lab_write_boundary
run
info registers rax rdi rsi rdx rcx r11 rsp
x/18cb $rsi
x/i $rip
si
print $rax
finish
continue
```

At the first completed boundary, predict RAX=1 and RDX=18; compare the observed
descriptor and payload address with the caller. After the instruction, predict
RAX=18. Step later error and partial cases separately. Addresses and descriptor
numbers depend on the run. The supplied checker restores its own saved caller
state and checks call-site alignment; it is not part of the learner task.

## Completion and review

Record the initial exit 78, completed byte row, both error interfaces, observed
capacity and every partial-progress count. Explain RCX/R11 clobbering, preserved
registers, pointer advancement and full-pipe handling. A copied regression that
selects read instead of write must fail the first operation; restoring the
correct syscall must restore both contracts and the demo. Do not change the
checks to accept a synthetic return.

Independent study follows prediction, implementation, execution and explanation.
A guided session traces the first call together, then asks for the error and
partial-progress predictions before running them. Passing code checks does not
complete `trace.md`.

## Primary references

- [Linux syscall ABI and the libc syscall function](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/syscall.2.html)
- [Linux write semantics](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/write.2.html)
- [Linux pipes and nonblocking writes](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/pipe.7.html)
- [Pipe capacity queries](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/F_GETPIPE_SZ.2const.html)
- [Linux v6.12 x86-64 syscall table](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.12/arch/x86/entry/syscalls/syscall_64.tbl)
- [glibc x86-64 syscall and error conversion implementation](https://github.com/bminor/glibc/blob/glibc-2.40/sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/x86_64/sysdep.h)

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(OwnedSyscallEvidence LANGUAGES C ASM)
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_C_EXTENSIONS OFF)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)
enable_testing()
add_executable(app main.c routine.S)
add_executable(contracts tests.c routine.S abi_checks.S)

endforeach()

# The fourth syscall argument and owned file creation

This extension follows four arguments across the C function ABI and the Linux
kernel ABI. Observe the permissions of an actual created file, compare raw
errors with libc, then explain why a returned descriptor alone does not prove
that the requested operation was performed correctly.

## Environment and files

Use ordinary-user Linux x86-64 with the System V AMD64 function ABI, GNU
assembler Intel syntax, C17, CMake 3.20+, Clang or GCC, GDB and strace. Confirm
the target with `uname -s` and `uname -m`. Windows uses an x86-64 WSL Linux
distribution; macOS uses an x86-64 Linux VM or lab.

Each role contains `routine.S`, `main.c`, `lab.h`, `tests.c`, `abi_checks.S`,
`CMakeLists.txt` and `trace.md`. Keep the files and this guide together after
export. Work in `starter` and save that attempt before opening the separate
reference. The browser is the editor and export path; Linux performs execution.

The two roles differ only in the named `SYSCALL_ARG4` task in `routine.S`.
The starter already enters the kernel with the correct syscall number, but it
deliberately clears the fourth kernel argument. Keep the supplied callers,
checks and requested permissions unchanged while completing that transfer.

## Follow the arguments across both boundaries

The wrapper's fixed four-argument interface is:

```c
long lab_openat(long directory, const char *path,
                long flags, unsigned long mode);
```

The C caller supplies those values in RDI, RSI, RDX and RCX. Linux x86-64 uses
RDI, RSI, RDX and R10 for the corresponding syscall arguments and syscall number
257 in RAX. Move the fourth value before the boundary. The boundary overwrites
RCX and R11; those are caller-saved registers. The original stack state and
RBX, RBP and R12–R15 still belong to the C function contract.

Here `path` is a readable zero-terminated name relative to the owned directory
descriptor. Flags select write access, exclusive creation and close-on-exec
behavior. Mode is used when creating a new file. Octal 0600 gives the owner read
and write bits; octal 0400 gives only the owner read bit. In decimal these are
384 and 256, so distinguish the display base from the underlying argument.

A successful raw result is a nonnegative descriptor; an error is a negative
kernel error code. This assembly wrapper does not convert errors into libc's
-1/`errno` convention. Capture the returned value and the separately stored
`errno` sentinel before another library call can change the observation.

## Own the complete experiment

The driver creates a unique `/tmp/assembly-openat-XXXXXX` directory using
`mkdtemp`, then opens that directory. All experiment paths are fixed relative
names inside it. No user-supplied external path is opened or replaced.

Within this single-threaded process, the driver temporarily selects umask 077
and restores its previous value during cleanup. The shell's mask is a separate
process state. On the ordinary local lab filesystem, the requested owner bits
remain while group/other bits are masked. Default filesystem ACLs can also
affect permission creation; use the documented plain local lab environment
when reproducing these exact mode comparisons.

The actual calls proceed as follows:

1. Create `owned-note` with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` and requested mode 0600.
2. Inspect the opened descriptor with `fstat` and compare actual mode bits.
3. Try exclusive creation of the same name and observe `-EEXIST`.
4. Open `missing/note` without creation and observe `-ENOENT`.
5. Compare the existing-name failure with libc `openat`, which returns -1 and
   sets `errno` to `EEXIST`.
6. Close owned descriptors, unlink the owned note, restore the process mask,
   and remove the temporary directory on both the success and failure paths.

The untouched starter can create a file and return a descriptor. Its supplied
fourth argument is zero, so `fstat` reports mode 0000 rather than 0600. The
driver records that mismatch, cleans up and exits 78. An already opened
descriptor can remain usable even when pathname permission bits are zero;
observe the metadata rather than treating the descriptor as proof of correct
permissions. Do not add a later chmod to hide the argument error.

After completion, the first row is:

```text
raw-create mode=0600 requested=0600 errno=123
```

The error row prints target-defined numeric values for raw `EEXIST` and `ENOENT`
alongside libc's -1 and positive `EEXIST`. Raw calls preserve the sentinel 123.
`--changed` requests 0400 instead and must report that actual mode. Descriptor
numbers, directory suffixes and instruction addresses vary between runs.

## Build and verify the selected role

From the extracted project directory:

```sh
cmake -S starter -B build-first -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_ASM_COMPILER=clang
cmake --build build-first --parallel 1
ctest --test-dir build-first --output-on-failure
./build-first/app
```

Keep the untouched failure. Complete only the fourth-argument transfer, then
configure a fresh `build-completed` directory. Require CTest, `app` and
`app --changed` to succeed. Build `solution` separately. Repeat completed roles
in Release and with both compiler options set to `gcc`, using separate build
folders. The checks remain active without C assertions in Release builds.

The contract program creates three actual files in turn with requested modes
0400, 0600 and 0700, verifies all three metadata results, checks three existing
name errors plus missing-parent and invalid-descriptor errors, and checks six
preserved registers. It unlinks each created file before the next case.

## Inspect the actual instruction and kernel operation

```sh
objdump -d -Mintel --disassemble=lab_openat build-completed/app
strace -f -yy -s 256 -e trace=openat,mkdir,rmdir,fstat,newfstatat,close,unlinkat,umask -o observed-openat.strace ./build-completed/app
gdb ./build-completed/app
```

Use a fresh trace filename for a changed or regression run. Separate the C
runtime's library-loading opens from the experiment's `owned-note` and
`missing/note` operations. Strace renders kernel errors using symbolic error
notation; compare that presentation with the raw return recorded by the caller.

In GDB:

```text
set disassembly-flavor intel
break *lab_openat_boundary
run
info registers rax rdi rsi rdx rcx r10 r11 rsp
x/s $rsi
x/i $rip
si
print $rax
finish
continue
```

At the first completed boundary, predict RAX=257 and R10=384. The pathname is
`owned-note`; RDI is this run's directory descriptor. Record the actual flags
and fourth argument before the instruction, then the returned descriptor and
the caller's independent metadata observation. Compare the starter's R10=0
with the completed value. The supplied ABI checker is an observer, not a file
creation workaround or a learner task.

## Completion and explanation

Complete `trace.md` with the original wrong mode, the corrected mode, the 0400
changed case, both raw errors and the libc comparison. Explain the two register
tables, the role of the process mask, exclusive creation and the full cleanup
sequence. A copied regression that clears R10 again must reproduce the wrong
mode and fail unchanged checks. Restoring the argument transfer must restore
both the contracts and the demo.

Independent study follows prediction, edit, execution and explanation. A guided
walkthrough pauses at the boundary and asks for the metadata prediction before
continuing. Passing runtime checks does not complete the written trace.

## Primary references

- [Linux syscall argument registers](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/syscall.2.html)
- [Linux open/openat creation, flags and permissions](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/open.2.html)
- [Linux v6.12 x86-64 syscall table](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.12/arch/x86/entry/syscalls/syscall_64.tbl)
- [glibc x86-64 fourth-argument transfer and error conversion](https://github.com/bminor/glibc/blob/glibc-2.40/sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/x86_64/sysdep.h)

# Syscall evidence worksheet

## Prediction
Record the function arguments, syscall number, kernel argument registers and
the distinction between a raw negative return and libc errno conversion.

## Observation
Record target, compiler, build profile, source role, command and exit status.
Capture the actual SYSCALL entry registers, return value and next instruction.
Keep the original unfinished result and the completed result in separate rows.

## Changed case
Record the changed payload or requested mode, actual transferred bytes or file
permissions, the observed errors and the reason the caller stops or continues.

## Ownership and cleanup
Identify only descriptors and temporary paths created by this process. Record
their close/unlink/rmdir evidence; distinguish a full pipe from a failed syscall.

## Explanation
Connect the observed kernel boundary to the C function ABI and libc wrapper.
Explain the controlled regression and why a passing build alone is insufficient.
